title: Checkpoint: Currents and Climate
objective: After this level you can explain how ocean currents shape climate.
summary: Follow one parcel of warm water: pushed by wind, carried north by the Gulf Stream, sunk into a 1,000-year conveyor. Currents spread Earth's heat.

cards.headline: Follow one parcel of warm water, and you'll travel the whole chapter.
cards.body: Its trip ties together the winds, the Gulf Stream and the slow deep sea. Along the way, you'll see why currents and climate are really one system.

cards.fact: Ocean currents carry warm water away from the equator and cold water from the poles, evening out Earth's heat.
cards.context: It's the planet's central heating, with pipes thousands of kilometers long. Every level in this chapter is part of that plumbing.

cards.headline: The trip
cards.body: Winds push our parcel along the surface into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north along Florida and then northeast across the Atlantic. In the cold far north it hands its heat to the air, and westerly winds carry that warmth to Europe. Now cold and salty, it sinks and joins the deep conveyor, where one lap takes about 1,000 years.

cards.headline: Heat, carbon and everything else
cards.body: The whole time, the ocean is doing climate's heavy lifting. It has taken up about 91% of the extra heat and about 30% of the carbon dioxide released into the air. Warm seas of at least 26.5°C fuel hurricanes, and the gyres gather our plastic into patches of microplastics. Currents and climate: one system.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How ocean currents act as the planet's central heating, carrying warmth away from the equator.
Why wind and Earth's spin bend surface currents into giant loops that also gather plastic.
How cold, salty water sinking in the far North Atlantic powers the ocean's slow deep conveyor.
How the ocean soaks up extra heat and carbon dioxide, and why that raises seas and makes them more acidic.

questions.prompt: Currents and Climate recap: what do ocean currents do for Earth's heat?

options.label: Move warm water from the equator, cold from the poles
Trap all of the planet's heat at the equator
options.rationale: Currents spread heat away from the equator.

options.label: Carry heat straight down into the sea floor
options.rationale: They move heat around the globe, not just down.

options.label: Nothing: the air does all of the heat moving
options.rationale: Currents carry warm and cold water around the planet.

questions.explanation: Ocean currents carry warm water from the equator and cold water from the poles, spreading heat around the planet.

questions.prompt: Currents and Climate recap: in what order does our warm parcel travel?

options.label: It sinks first, then rides the Gulf Stream, then the wind moves it
options.rationale: Sinking comes last, once it's cold and salty.

options.label: Wind-driven current, Gulf Stream north, then sinking into the conveyor
It rides the Gulf Stream south to the equator, then sinks
options.rationale: The Gulf Stream carries it north.

options.label: It sinks at the equator and rises near Norway
options.rationale: It sinks in the cold far north.

questions.explanation: Winds push it into the Gulf Stream, which carries it north; there it cools, turns salty and sinks into the conveyor.

questions.prompt: Currents and Climate recap, from Level 33: what makes water sink in the far North Atlantic?

options.label: It is warm and fresh from the Gulf Stream
The Moon's pull drags the water down
options.rationale: The Moon drives tides, not the conveyor.

options.label: It's cold and extra salty, so it's dense
Passing hurricanes push the water under
options.rationale: Storms aren't the engine of the conveyor.

questions.explanation: Chilled by Arctic air and left saltier as sea ice forms, the water is dense enough to sink.

questions.prompt: Currents and Climate recap, from Level 35: how warm must the sea be to fuel a hurricane?

options.label: At least about 16.5°C
At least about 21.5°C
At least about 26.5°C
At least about 31.5°C

questions.explanation: Hurricanes need seawater of at least 26.5°C, reaching down about 50 m.

questions.prompt: Currents and Climate recap, from Level 39: why can't satellites see the Great Pacific Garbage Patch?

options.label: It's mostly tiny microplastics
It only forms at night, when satellites can't see
It's hidden under the Arctic sea ice
options.rationale: It lies between Hawaii and California, far from sea ice.

options.label: It's made of clear glass, which is invisible

questions.explanation: The patch is mostly microplastics smaller than 5 mm, spread like pepper in soup, so satellite images don't show it.
